description: Lead, cadmium, mercury, nickel and chromium in pea protein powders and concentrates, with the separate record for garden pea fruit, applicable European maxima, and what a lot test needs to show.
search_limitations: Open literature and the HMI library were searched for pea protein, pea protein isolate, Pisum sativum and pulse-protein metal studies.
Supplier notices and company certificates were excluded.
The 2009 Canadian field-pea article is closed and was not table-extracted.
Clean Label Project market reports are not peer-reviewed and were not used as concentrations.

intro: Pea protein here is the powdered protein fraction, not the whole pea and not a blend that only lists pea among other ingredients.
Two retail pea powders bought in Ireland in 2016 and 2017 contained 15.4 and 40.6 µg/kg cadmium and 22.2 and 22.5 µg/kg lead, on the powder as sold.
Total mercury in those powders was 4.3 µg/kg and below 0.2 µg/kg, and arsenic was not measured.

Two anonymized pea concentrates had nickel at 268.27 and 585.49 µg/kg and total chromium at 78.97 and 114.11 µg/kg, with cadmium and lead not detected under a ppb heading whose footnotes do not restate the unit.
The European Union sets 100 µg/kg cadmium for proteins from pulses and 40 µg/kg for other pulses, so the protein row is the one that matches this ingredient.

facets.label: Metals measured
sentences: Metals measured in the powders are lead, cadmium, total mercury, nickel, total chromium and tin, and the fruit series adds total arsenic.
The Irish powders are single retail packages, so each metal is one value per package rather than a mean of many lots.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
The concentrates report means and standard deviations from duplicate purchases, not a market distribution.
lopezcalabozo2025-vegetable-protein-concentrates
Arsenic and mercury were not part of the concentrate mineral table, so a blank there is an unmeasured cell.
lopezcalabozo2025-vegetable-protein-concentrates
Garden pea fruit from Egypt is a different form in the table, reported on a dry-weight basis after oven drying, and it is not a protein powder.
galal2021-heavy-metals-pisum-sativum

facets.label: Main drivers
sentences: Main drivers are the form, the basis, and whether the sample is a retail powder, a concentrate, or pea fruit from an industrial district.
Within one Irish survey, the two pea powders sat above most whey powders for cadmium and below the two mixed plant powders.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
Lead in those pea powders was about 22 µg/kg, while whey lead in the same study ran from 0.8 to 88.4 µg/kg, so pea was not the high-lead tail.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
Polluted-site pea fruit in Egypt carried far more cadmium and lead than unpolluted-site fruit from the same study, which shows soil and site can dominate the plant.
galal2021-heavy-metals-pisum-sativum
Purchase country is not growing origin: the Irish and Spanish samples do not name where the peas were grown.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
lopezcalabozo2025-vegetable-protein-concentrates

facets.label: Practical framing
sentences: Practical framing starts with the limit that matches the legal category of the lot, not with a single number borrowed from whole peas.
Proteins from pulses are at 100 µg/kg cadmium in the European table, and pulses other than that protein row are at 40 µg/kg.
eu-2021-1323-cadmium-foodstuffs-amendment
A food supplement has a separate cadmium maximum of 1,000 µg/kg as placed on the market, which applies when the product is sold as a supplement.
eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels
Nickel in pulses other than dry beans and lupins is 4,000 µg/kg from 1 July 2025, and that row is the pulse, not a protein-from-pulses row.
eu-2024-1987-nickel-maximum-levels
A useful lot report names the form, the basis, the method, and a quantification limit well below the maximum that applies.

summary: Pea protein on this page is the powdered protein fraction of field pea, sold as an isolate, a concentrate, or a retail powder.
Whole peas and multi-ingredient blends are discussed only where a study measured them, and they are not pooled with the isolate.
Two retail pea powders bought online and in Cork, Ireland, in 2016 and 2017 contained 40.6 and 15.4 µg/kg cadmium and 22.2 and 22.5 µg/kg lead, as sold.
Total mercury in those two powders was 4.3 µg/kg and below 0.2 µg/kg, total chromium was 289.2 and 210.7 µg/kg, and total tin was 26.7 and 329.7 µg/kg.
Two anonymized commercial pea concentrates, each bought twice, showed nickel means of 585.49 and 268.27 µg/kg and total chromium means of 78.97 and 114.11 µg/kg, with cadmium and lead not detected.
The European cadmium maximum that names proteins from pulses is 100 µg/kg, set beside 40 µg/kg for pulses other than that protein row.
For a buyer the first distinction is the material: isolate or concentrate versus whole seed, frozen peas, or a blend.
The second is the basis, because a dry-weight fruit result and an as-sold powder result are not the same measurement.
The third is the reporting limit, because a non-detect is an interval up to that limit and not a measured zero.
The Irish powders and the Spanish concentrates do not record the country where the peas were grown, so they cannot rank Canada, China, or the European Union as growing origins.
Lot testing describes the lot in hand, and it does not remove cadmium, lead, or any other element from the powder.
identity: This page covers pea protein as a food ingredient: the protein-rich powder made from field pea, including isolates and concentrates sold as such.
The Irish evidence is two retail products the authors classified as pea, among 36 protein powders that also included whey, soy, casein, and mixed plant powders.
The concentrate evidence is two anonymized commercial pea protein concentrates, bought from online shops and analyzed beside rice and soybean concentrates in the same paper.
A third form in the table is garden pea fruit, oven-dried, from farms in South Cairo and Giza, which is the pea pod's seed tissue as a vegetable and not a separated protein.
Frozen boiled green peas in the US Total Diet Study, and Canadian field pea seed in a 2009 grain baseline, are cited as other materials and are not rows of this powder.
An isolate is a higher-protein powder than a concentrate, but these studies do not print a protein percentage for the packages they tested, so the page keeps the authors' own names.
A retail powder can also contain flavor, sweetener, or another protein, and the Irish paper identifies the two pea products as pea rather than as a named blend.
Plant powders that list pea together with rice or seeds are blends, and a metal in the blend cannot be assigned to the pea fraction.
Dry-weight, as-sold, and unstated results stay in separate comparisons, and this page does not apply a moisture conversion.
Transferring a whole-pea concentration onto an isolate, or an isolate concentration onto frozen peas, would treat different foods as one food.
occurrence: The table lists every extracted result for this page: the Irish pea powders, the two pea concentrates, and the Egyptian garden pea fruit means.
On the Irish powders as sold, cadmium was 40.6 µg/kg in one package and 15.4 µg/kg in the other, and lead was 22.2 and 22.5 µg/kg.

Total mercury was 4.3 µg/kg and below 0.2 µg/kg, total chromium was 289.2 and 210.7 µg/kg, and total tin was 26.7 and 329.7 µg/kg, the last of those being the highest tin the study reported in any powder.
The concentrate table, printed in a ppb block, gives nickel 585.49 ± 47.94 and 268.27 ± 35.21 and total chromium 78.97 ± 11.24 and 114.11 ± 31.83, with cadmium and lead marked not detected.
The footnotes give detection limits below 0.015 and below 0.026 without restating the unit, so those non-detects are not converted here into a food concentration of zero.
Garden pea fruit, dry weight, is the other block in the table, and it is labeled as fruit so it is not read as a powder.
Unpolluted-site fruit means were 8.9 mg/kg lead, 2.6 mg/kg cadmium, 0.03 mg/kg arsenic, 0.9 mg/kg chromium, and 0.9 mg/kg nickel.
Polluted-site fruit means were 121.0 mg/kg lead, 1,025.0 mg/kg cadmium, 0.1 mg/kg arsenic, 19.8 mg/kg chromium, and 24.7 mg/kg nickel.
Those fruit values are total metals on a dry-weight basis after oven drying, arsenic is not speciated, and the polluted farms received industrial and municipal waste.

Few of these powder rows can be rated against an HMI reference, because a reference needs at least four compatible medians or sample values for the same form and basis, and the method sentence is not repeated under every metal.
pathways: Cadmium and lead reach peas from the soil and from dust or waste deposited on the crop, and the element remains in the tissue because cooking and drying do not destroy it.

A review by FDA scientists describes diet as the main cadmium exposure for people who are not exposed at work and do not smoke, and it identifies soil pH, cultivar, and fertilizer choice as levers on how much the plant takes up.
That review's highest mean foods in the US Total Diet Study were not peas, which is a reminder that a concentrated protein ingredient and a boiled vegetable are different exposure questions.

Field pea is a pulse, and pulses are known to take cadmium up from soil, but the size of that uptake is a property of the soil, the variety, and the season, not a single concentration for every origin.

No powder study in this library paired the metal in the seed with the metal in the isolate made from that seed, so the pathway into the powder is inferred from the crop and from the process, not measured end to end.
The direct crop comparison on this page is garden pea grown in South Cairo and Giza in the winter of 2017.
Fruit from farms that received waste from cement, iron and steel, brick, and fertilizer works contained much more lead, cadmium, chromium, and nickel than fruit from the study's unpolluted farms.
The unpolluted fruit was not a clean commercial baseline either: 2.6 mg/kg cadmium and 8.9 mg/kg lead, dry weight, are far above the Irish retail powders.

The authors report bioaccumulation factors above 1 for several metals at the polluted sites, which means the plant tissues held more metal than the soil measurement they used, but that factor is for those sites and not a universal pea constant.
Industrial fruit and a retail isolate answer different questions, and the fruit series is here to show how strongly site can move the crop, not to describe protein sold for food manufacture.
variation: Inside the Irish survey, using one method and one purchase market, the two pea powders are not the high end for every metal.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
Pea cadmium was 15.4 and 40.6 µg/kg, soy was 20.7 and 23.4 µg/kg, mixed plant was 45.1 and 58.1 µg/kg, and the 27 whey powders ran from below 0.61 to 23.2 µg/kg.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
Pea lead was 22.2 and 22.5 µg/kg, while whey lead ran from 0.8 to 88.4 µg/kg and one mixed plant powder was 49.5 µg/kg, so the highest lead package in that study was whey.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
The highest total mercury was 18.4 µg/kg in a mixed plant powder, against 4.3 µg/kg and below 0.2 µg/kg in the pea powders.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
Two pea packages cannot rank a category, and they do not identify a growing region, because the paper records where the powders were bought and not where the crop was grown.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
The concentrate paper allows a within-study look at pea versus rice protein, still with only two products of each and with the mineral basis unstated.
lopezcalabozo2025-vegetable-protein-concentrates
Both pea concentrates were not detected for lead, while one rice concentrate contained 175.40 ppb lead and the other was not detected.
lopezcalabozo2025-vegetable-protein-concentrates
Nickel overlapped: pea 268.27 and 585.49 ppb, rice 240.22 and 604.54 ppb, so neither protein was uniformly higher.
lopezcalabozo2025-vegetable-protein-concentrates
Total chromium was lower in the pea concentrates (78.97 and 114.11 ppb) than in the rice concentrates (208.98 and 627.11 ppb) in that small set.
lopezcalabozo2025-vegetable-protein-concentrates

Hungary adds a different comparison: plant powders that included pea with rice or seeds were not detected for arsenic, cadmium, mercury, and lead, but the detection limits were not printed, and aluminum was higher in the plant powders than in most whey powders.
horvath2025-hungary-protein-powders-metals
A Canada, China, and European Union ranking of pea protein isolate is not supported by the measurements in hand.

The Canadian Grain Commission baseline of field pea seed reports, in its abstract, a mean cadmium of 0.023 mg/kg, with arsenic and lead below 0.050 mg/kg and mercury below 0.002 mg/kg, and the full sample table was not available.
gawalko2009-canadian-field-peas-trace-elements
That abstract describes whole seed, not an isolate, and it does not give the number of samples or the years, so it is not an occurrence row and not a sourcing preference.
gawalko2009-canadian-field-peas-trace-elements
No eligible study here measured pea protein isolate grown in China, or separated European-grown isolate from European retail of unknown origin.
Until origin is printed with the lot, the lowest observed package in one shop is only the lowest package in that shop.
processing: Separating protein from pea removes starch and fiber and dries what remains, which can raise the metal concentration per kilogram if the metal stays with the protein and the discarded fraction held less.
That is a mass-balance expectation, not a result from these papers, because none of them analyzed the seed, the isolate, and the side streams from the same lot.
The European cadmium table is the regulatory trace of that expectation: pulses other than proteins from pulses are 0.040 mg/kg, and proteins from pulses are 0.10 mg/kg.
The protein maximum is 2.5 times the pulse maximum, which is legal room for a more concentrated ingredient, not a measured yield from a factory trial.
The Irish pea powders at 15.4 and 40.6 µg/kg cadmium sit under the 100 µg/kg protein row, and that comparison is two packages, not a compliance rate.

Wet fractionation, which solubilizes protein and then precipitates it, and dry fractionation, which separates by air classification, can move minerals differently, and this library does not contain a head-to-head metal balance for pea.
Heat does not destroy lead, cadmium, arsenic, or mercury, so roasting or cooking changes a concentration only by moving water or by parting a fraction that carries the metal.
Drying a wet vegetable raises the concentration per kilogram without adding metal, which is one reason a dry powder and a boiled pea are not compared by the raw number.
The Egyptian fruit was oven-dried before analysis, so its milligrams per kilogram are dry weight and would look lower on a fresh pea that is mostly water.
A process claim that an isolate step removes cadmium needs the before and after on the same lot, with the basis and the yield stated, and that pair is not in these studies.
controls: No study in this library measured a treatment that lowered lead, cadmium, arsenic, or mercury in pea protein and reported the size of that change.
The crop literature points upstream: soil pH, cultivar, and fertilizer choice change how much cadmium a plant takes up, which is the step that keeps the metal out of the seed.
Those levers were not tested on the retail powders or the concentrates reviewed here, so they are a research direction and not a quantified benefit for this ingredient.
The Egyptian contrast shows the other side of siting, because fruit beside cement, iron, and fertilizer works held far more metal than the study's other farms.
Choosing a growing area away from that kind of waste is supported as a difference in that study, and it is not a universal map of clean regions for protein isolate.
Once the powder is made, the verifiable control in this evidence is lot testing against the maximum that applies to the legal category of the product.
A specification sheet that repeats a target, without a method and a result for the lot, does not show what the lot contains.
Washing or cooking advice drawn from vegetables does not transfer to a dry protein powder that has already been milled and dried.
Blending pea with a lower-metal protein would change the blend, and it would not change the pea fraction, and this page does not have a measured dilution trial.
The absence of a measured removal step is recorded as a gap, not as evidence that no control exists in the factory.
tradeoffs: Metals do not move together, so a lot that is lower in lead can be higher in cadmium, nickel, or chromium.
In the Irish set the highest lead powder was whey, while the highest cadmium powders were mixed plant, and the pea powders were mid-pack for lead and higher than most whey for cadmium.
In the concentrate set, pea was the lower total chromium pair and not a lower nickel pair, and one rice concentrate carried detected lead while the pea concentrates did not.
A blend that looks low in one metal can still carry another metal from rice, cocoa, or a flavor ingredient, and the pea share of that blend is not identified.
Avoiding an industrial waste site lowered fruit metals in one Egyptian study, and that choice is not a measured cost, yield, or protein-quality result.
testing: The powders in the Irish study were microwave-digested and measured by sector-field inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, with results reported per kilogram of powder as sold.
The concentrates were microwave-digested in nitric acid and measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, and the paper does not state a dry-weight or as-sold basis for the mineral block.
A lot report that a buyer can use names the form, the basis, the analyte, the method, the result, and the quantification limit.
For a 100 µg/kg cadmium maximum, a quantification limit of a few micrograms per kilogram can show the distance to the maximum, and a limit of 200 µg/kg cannot.
Total chromium is not hexavalent chromium, and total arsenic is not inorganic arsenic, unless the method speciates them.

The concentrate footnotes print detection limits below 0.015 and below 0.026 under the ppb heading and do not repeat the unit, so this page does not treat 0.015 µg/kg as a demonstrated food limit of quantification.
The Hungarian plant powders were below detection for arsenic, cadmium, mercury, and lead, and the paper does not print those detection limits, so the non-detect cannot be placed on a number line.
Arsenic was not in the Irish method at all, which matters if the product is a pea and rice blend, because rice is the ingredient that usually drives inorganic arsenic.
A single composite or a single package is not a year's production, and the Irish design is one analysis per product.
Ask for the lot identity on the certificate, the digestion, the basis, and the limit of quantification, and do not accept a target copied from a sales specification as if it were a result.
procurement: The cadmium row that names proteins from pulses is 0.10 mg/kg, which is 100 µg/kg, in the European amendment that created that split.
Pulses other than proteins from pulses are 0.040 mg/kg, which is 40 µg/kg, and that lower row is the seed and not the protein ingredient.

Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 is the instrument now in force for contaminant maxima, and its food-supplement row sets 1.0 mg/kg cadmium, 1,000 µg/kg, for supplements other than the seaweed and bivalve row.
A pea protein ingredient in a food is not automatically a food supplement, so the buyer has to know which legal category the lot is placed on the market under.
Nickel maxima added in 2024 set 4.0 mg/kg for pulses except dry beans and dry lupins, applying from 1 July 2025, and there is no separate nickel row for proteins from pulses.
Processed foods that are not themselves a listed category are handled by the concentration and dilution rules of the contaminants regulation, not by inventing a new number.

The nickel measured in the two pea concentrates, about 268 to 585 µg/kg, is numerically below 4,000 µg/kg, and that is not a compliance test, because the basis is unstated and the legal row is the pulse.
This page did not verify a United States maximum written for pea protein or for proteins from pulses, and the Total Diet Study figures for boiled peas are monitoring results, not limits.

A purchasing specification should name lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic when rice is in the formula, total mercury, and nickel, each with a quantification limit below the maximum that applies.
Origin language on a contract is only as good as the lot record that ties the powder to a harvest region, which these retail studies do not provide.
product: The Irish study estimated hazard indexes for a 70 kg adult at one serving and at three servings a day, using the authors' reference doses.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
At one serving a day, no powder in the study had a hazard index above 1.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
At three servings a day, ten powders did, including one of the two pea powders, a mixed plant powder, a casein powder, and several whey powders.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals

The same paper's cadmium cancer-risk screen at three servings a day included that pea powder among four products the authors still described as within a range they called acceptable, while warning that high intake over a lifetime could raise risk.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
Those calculations are the authors' model for the packages they bought, and they are not an intake for a child, a different serving size, or a different product.
Boiled frozen green peas in the US Total Diet Study are a useful contrast because they are the vegetable, mostly water, eaten as a side dish.
fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020
Across three composites, cadmium was detected in two, with a reported maximum of 3.2 µg/kg and a reporting limit of 1 µg/kg.
fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020
Lead was not detected at a reporting limit of 4 µg/kg, total mercury was not detected at 1 µg/kg, and total arsenic was not detected at 3 µg/kg.
fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020
A 30 gram scoop of dry protein is not a serving of boiled peas, so those non-detects do not describe the powder.
Concentration in the food and intake by a person remain separate: this page does not multiply a powder result by a consumption survey to produce a population dose.
The labeled scoop masses in the Irish table are 30 g for pea sample 2 and 10 g for pea sample 12.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
At those scoops, sample 2 carries 0.666 µg lead and 1.218 µg cadmium, and sample 12 carries 0.225 µg lead and 0.154 µg cadmium.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals

California's oral maximum allowable dose level for lead, for reproductive toxicity, is 0.5 µg/day, so one 30 g scoop of either pea powder is above that daily level and the labeled 10 g scoop of sample 12 is not.
oehha-lead-prop65-listing
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
The oral cadmium level is 4.1 µg/day, and both labeled scoops are below it (1.218 µg and 0.154 µg).
oehha-cadmium-prop65-madl-2001
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals

Dividing those daily levels by 0.030 kg gives about 16.7 µg/kg lead and about 137 µg/kg cadmium as the powder concentrations at which one 30 g scoop equals the daily level, which is a scoop check and not a food maximum or a full-day diet.
oehha-lead-prop65-listing
oehha-cadmium-prop65-madl-2001
assessment: The occurrence rows come from the Irish retail survey, the concentrate mineral table, and the Egyptian fruit table, each read for the pea material the paper actually measured.

Plant-protein blends, a unit-unresolved survey of vegan powders, and an Indian labeling study that pooled pea with soy were not entered as pea protein concentrations, because the pea fraction or the unit could not be defended.
Industry market reports that are not peer-reviewed and do not publish a concentration table were not used as numbers.
Supplier notices and company certificates of analysis were excluded, including any notice written for a single manufacturer's pea protein.
The 2009 Canadian field-pea article remains closed: the abstract means are cited with that limit, and they are not rows.
What is still missing is a multi-lot survey of pea protein isolate with growing origin, basis, and quantification limits for lead, cadmium, inorganic arsenic, and total mercury.
A paired seed and isolate from the same lots would show whether protein separation concentrates cadmium, which the legal 40 versus 100 µg/kg split only allows for and does not measure.
Two Irish packages and two concentrates are enough to show the ingredient is not free of these elements, and they are not enough for a rated reference or a regional ranking.
The Egyptian fruit series is strong evidence about a polluted agricultural district and weak evidence about commercial protein.
Corrections to a misread table, a retrieved Canadian full text, or a new origin-linked survey should reopen the affected paragraphs.

ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals

lopezcalabozo2025-vegetable-protein-concentrates
Nickel means were 585.49 and 268.27 µg/kg and total chromium means were 78.97 and 114.11 µg/kg, with cadmium and lead not detected.
lopezcalabozo2025-vegetable-protein-concentrates
A non-detect is not a measured zero when the detection limit's unit is not restated, which is the case for those concentrate footnotes.

faqs.question: How do cadmium and lead get into peas?
sentences: The plant takes cadmium and lead up from soil, and contaminated dust or waste can add more, which is why site matters.
schaefer2020-cadmium-mitigation-strategies
Soil pH, the variety, and the fertilizer program change uptake, according to a review of dietary cadmium by FDA scientists.
schaefer2020-cadmium-mitigation-strategies
In South Cairo and Giza, pea fruit beside cement, iron, brick, and fertilizer works held 1,025 mg/kg cadmium and 121 mg/kg lead, dry weight.
galal2021-heavy-metals-pisum-sativum
Fruit from the study's other farms held 2.6 mg/kg cadmium and 8.9 mg/kg lead, dry weight, which is lower than the polluted fruit and still high next to retail powders.

Those fruit results explain the crop pathway, and they are not the concentration of a protein isolate.

faqs.question: Does making an isolate concentrate the metals?
sentences: Protein separation discards starch and fiber and dries the protein fraction, so a metal that follows the protein can be higher per kilogram in the powder than in the seed.
No paper in this set measured the same lot as seed and as isolate, so that concentration is not a measured factor here.
European law sets cadmium at 40 µg/kg for pulses and at 100 µg/kg for proteins from pulses, which leaves room for a more concentrated ingredient.
eu-2021-1323-cadmium-foodstuffs-amendment
The Irish pea powders at 15.4 and 40.6 µg/kg cadmium are under the protein row, and two packages do not show how often that happens.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
Heat does not destroy the elements, so a roasting step is not, by itself, a removal step.
schaefer2020-cadmium-mitigation-strategies

faqs.question: Are Canadian, Chinese, or European peas lower?
sentences: None of the powder studies records the country where the peas were grown, so Canada, China, and the European Union cannot be ranked as isolate origins.
The Irish powders were bought in Ireland, and the concentrates were bought online for a laboratory in Spain.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
lopezcalabozo2025-vegetable-protein-concentrates
A Canadian Grain Commission paper on field pea seed reports a mean cadmium of 0.023 mg/kg in its abstract, with arsenic and lead below 0.050 mg/kg.
gawalko2009-canadian-field-peas-trace-elements
The full article is closed, the sample table was not read, and the material is whole seed rather than isolate.
gawalko2009-canadian-field-peas-trace-elements
A sourcing preference needs origin on the lot, the same form, and the same basis, and those three are not together in this library.

faqs.question: How do pea powders compare with whey and other plant powders?
sentences: In the Irish survey the two pea powders were higher in cadmium than most of the 27 whey powders and lower than the two mixed plant powders.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
Whey cadmium ran from below 0.61 to 23.2 µg/kg, pea was 15.4 and 40.6, and mixed plant was 45.1 and 58.1.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
Lead did not follow cadmium: pea was about 22 µg/kg and the highest lead result was 88.4 µg/kg in a whey powder.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
Among two pea and two rice concentrates, detected lead was in one rice product, and total chromium was higher in both rice products than in either pea product.

Two or four products are a comparison inside one study, not a ranking of the world's pea protein against the world's whey.

eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels
Food supplements have a cadmium maximum of 1.0 mg/kg as placed on the market, except the higher seaweed and bivalve supplement row.
eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels

eu-2024-1987-nickel-maximum-levels

faqs.question: What should a laboratory report include?
sentences: The report should name the form, such as isolate, concentrate, or blend, and the basis, such as as sold or dry weight.
It should list lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic if rice is in the product, total mercury, and nickel, each with its own result.
The quantification limit should sit well below the maximum that applies, for example well below 100 µg/kg where the protein cadmium row applies.
eu-2021-1323-cadmium-foodstuffs-amendment
The method should be an acid digestion and a mass-spectrometric or equivalent determination, with the lot identity on the same page.
ring2021-ireland-protein-powders-metals
A non-detect should show the limit, and a limit whose unit is not stated cannot be used as a food concentration.

faqs.question: Do the concentrate non-detects mean the cadmium is very low?
